raw_response.headline_result_summary: In this cross-sectional multilevel analysis of 3,047 piped-water households across 177 urban and peri-urban DHS clusters and 11 NWASCO-regulated commercial Water and Sewerage Companies (WSCs) in Zambia, 46.7% (reported as 47%; 95% CI: 44%–49% in text, 45%–49% in Abstract) of households experienced at least one full day of water service interruption in the preceding fortnight, ranging from 18.7% (Lukanga WSC) to 77.0% (Kafubu WSC). Across legal, tenure, and regulatory/utility dimensions, results are mixed depending on the focal exposure: (1) Housing tenure (home ownership: 'At least partly owns' vs. 'Does not own') was associated with significantly HIGHER odds of experiencing a water interruption (i.e., worse service continuity, contrary to the authors' hypothesis) in both adjusted multilevel models (Model 1 controlling for WSC dummies: OR = 1.31, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01; Model 2 controlling for cluster and provider covariates: OR = 1.32, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01), though borderline/non-significant in unadjusted weighted bivariate analysis (50.8% vs. 45.0%, chi-squared = 6.19, p = 0.05). (2) Statutory regulator (NWASCO) and utility (IBNET) operational metrics were strongly associated with interruptions in unadjusted chi-square tests (p < 0.001), but in adjusted multilevel Model 2 utility Non-Revenue Water (leakage/illegal connections) dropped out via backward elimination (p > 0.05) and Regulator LPCD had a null main effect (OR = 1.01, SE = 0.01) alongside small, opposing interactions (reducing interruptions in middle-wealth vs. poor clusters, OR = 0.97, p < 0.05; slightly increasing interruptions at higher provider-level GDP per capita, OR = 1.02, p < 0.01), while service-provider-area GDP per capita ($1,000s) strongly reduced interruptions (OR = 0.51, SE = 0.11, p < 0.01). (3) Controlling for household characteristics (Model 1), large inter-utility inequalities persisted relative to Lusaka WSC (1 WSC with significantly lower interruption odds [Lukanga OR = 0.36, p < 0.05], 4 WSCs significantly higher at p < 0.05 [Chambeshi, Kafubu, Luapula, Mulongo; ORs 2.43–8.02], 1 borderline at p < 0.10 [Nkana OR = 2.24], and 4 null). (4) Using a neighbour's tap or yard/public standpipe vs. water piped into dwelling was statistically null at p < 0.05 across all models (neighbour's tap OR = 1.33, p < 0.10 in Model 2 only).
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. CRITICAL OUTCOME POLARITY TRAP: On p. 7 the authors name the binary outcome variable 'user reported availability of piped water', yet it is coded 1 = water was NOT available for at least one full day in the past two weeks (an interruption/outage). Thus OR > 1 (positive raw sign) indicates MORE service interruptions = WORSE household continuity/access, and OR < 1 indicates FEWER interruptions = BETTER continuity/access. 2. COUNTER-HYPOTHESIS TENURE EFFECT: Home ownership ('At least partly owns' vs. 'Does not own', labelled 'tenure' in S13 Table) yields OR = 1.31–1.32 (p < 0.01) for interruptions—meaning formal home ownership is associated with WORSE continuity in adjusted models, contrary to the authors' hypothesis (p. 17), whereas unadjusted bivariate p = 0.05 (Table 1) is treated as non-significant (p > 0.05) on p. 10. 3. AUTHORS' OWN SIGN-FLIP ERROR ON NEIGHBOURHOOD WEALTH: In Table 4 (Model 2) and Results (p. 14), Middle neighbourhood wealth (vs. Poor) has a main-effect OR = 4.31* (SE = 3.29, p < 0.10, misstated as p < 0.01 on p. 14) and an interaction with Regulator LPCD of OR = 0.97** (p < 0.05); however, in Discussion (pp. 16–17) the authors invert the main-effect statement, claiming 'Households in mid-wealth clusters were less likely to experience an interruption than those in poor clusters' (which only holds conditional on high LPCD above ~48 LPCD). 4. BIVARIATE VS. MULTILEVEL ATTENUATION OF UTILITY/REGULATOR METRICS: Because there are only 11 WSCs across 3,047 households, unadjusted chi-square tests (Table 2) yield p < 0.001 for Non-Revenue Water, hrs/day, and LPCD; once cluster random effects (177 clusters) and covariates are modelled in Table 4, Non-Revenue Water drops out (p > 0.05) and Regulator LPCD has a null main effect (OR = 1.01, SE = 0.01). 5. TABLE TYPOS AND P-VALUE THRESHOLDS: Table 1 misprints the p-value for Provider (chi-squared = 245.87, df = 10) as 0.93 (copied from Household Wealth above it; Table 2 confirms p < 0.001). Several results highlighted in the Abstract/text (Piped to neighbour OR = 1.33*, Nkana WSC OR = 2.24*, Middle neighbourhood wealth OR = 4.31*, Tonga OR = 1.78*, Bemba OR = 1.88*) are only significant at p < 0.10, not p < 0.05. 6. CONDITIONING ON PIPED USERS: All rural households (n = 8,117) and urban non-piped households (n = 1,574) were excluded, so findings apply strictly to continuity among existing urban/peri-urban piped-water users, not access to a piped connection.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional observational study spatially linking georeferenced household survey data (2018 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey) with utility benchmarking data (2017 IBNET) and statutory regulator reports (2017/2018 NWASCO), analysed via survey-weighted bivariate chi-square tests and unweighted two-level multilevel logistic regression (households nested in DHS clusters)
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Urban and peri-urban piped drinking-water households in Zambia: n = 3,047 households nested within 177 DHS sampling clusters across 11 commercial Water and Sewerage Company (WSC) coverage areas (after excluding 8,117 rural households in 347 clusters, 47 households in 2 clusters missing GPS coordinates, 1,574 urban households not using piped drinking water, and 46 with unknown continuity)
